details:
VIGIL LUNA-01

Beyond Monitoring: Building a Future for Astronaut Healthcare Beyond Earth

Bringing continuous healthcare and human support to space missions.

PROJECT SUMMARY

Who looks after an astronaut when medical help from Earth is no longer just a phone call away?

VIGIL began with a simple question: how can we make sure astronauts receive proper healthcare during long missions, even when they are millions of kilometres away from Earth?

Inspired by a physician's perspective, we set out to explore what healthcare could look like beyond our planet. We wanted to build something that goes beyond collecting health measurements. Something that can help astronauts understand their health, keep track of changes and access support when they need it.

Our LUNA-01 demonstration brings this idea to life through synthetic astronaut health records, physiological trends, mission conditions, a Crew Health Map and four simulated Medical Companion roles: Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist and Psychologist.

But VIGIL is bigger than the software we have today. We imagine it eventually becoming the intelligence and coordination system behind a future space medical bay, bringing together automated laboratory testing, bone-health monitoring, robotic ultrasound, psychological support and specialised medical AI.

Our goal is to explore how reliable, accessible healthcare can travel with people, wherever humanity goes.

1. THE PROBLEM: HEALTHCARE BEYOND EARTH

When we think about space exploration, we often focus on rockets, spacecraft and the technology needed to reach distant worlds. But there is another challenge that deserves just as much attention: looking after the people who make those missions possible.

An astronaut is more than a set of numbers on a monitor. They are human beings who can experience fatigue, discomfort, stress, loneliness and illness. During a long-duration mission, these challenges can become even harder to manage because immediate medical support from Earth may not be available.

Spaceflight also brings its own health challenges. Changes in gravity can affect muscles and bones, while disrupted sleep, isolation and demanding schedules can influence both physical and psychological wellbeing.

Monitoring health measurements is important, but it is only part of the picture. Astronauts also need support that considers their medical history, changing circumstances and personal experiences.

This led us to ask:

What if astronauts could carry a healthcare companion with them, one that helps them understand their health and access support even when Earth is far away?

That question became the starting point for VIGIL.

2. OUR SOLUTION: VIGIL

VIGIL is an astronaut health-monitoring and support platform that we are developing around LUNA-01, a fictional mission to the lunar south pole.

Our current demonstration brings several ideas together:

- Mission-aware health monitoring: Tracks synthetic crew health measurements, personal baselines, sleep, activity and wellbeing throughout a simulated mission.

- Physiological trends: Helps users see how health indicators change over time instead of looking at individual readings in isolation.

- Crew Health Map: Shows shared numerical patterns across permitted crew records using predefined demonstration rules.

- Mission-control interface: Includes an interactive 3D lunar environment, mission phases, lander inspection and simulated interruptions in communication with Earth.

- Four Medical Companion roles: Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist and Psychologist, each representing a different aspect of astronaut healthcare.

- Medical references: Provides access to selected NASA Human Research Program material and links to the original sources.

- Personalised support research: A separate authenticated development prototype explores evidence-based responses and consent-controlled health memories.

We wanted VIGIL to bring together two important things: the awareness and organisation of mission control, and the continuity and understanding of a healthcare team.

3. THE HUMAN SIDE OF SPACE EXPLORATION

Physical health is only one part of an astronaut's wellbeing.

Imagine spending months away from family and friends, living in a confined environment and following demanding schedules with very little privacy. Even the most experienced astronauts can face psychological challenges in these conditions.

This is why we included a simulated Psychologist companion in VIGIL.

It represents our early exploration of how technology could support regular wellbeing check-ins, provide a space for supportive conversations and maintain continuity between interactions.

In the future, we would like to explore more personalised support through consent-based memory, culturally sensitive communication and scientifically reviewed psychological assessment methods.

We also recognise that healthcare is not the same for everyone. Certain needs, including menstrual, reproductive and sexual health, deserve appropriate attention and strong privacy protections rather than being overlooked by general monitoring systems.

Our intention is not to replace human relationships or professional mental healthcare. We want to explore how responsible technology can make support more accessible when direct human assistance is difficult to reach.

4. OUR FUTURE VISION: AN INTELLIGENT SPACE MEDICAL BAY

The current VIGIL application is only the beginning of what we hope to explore.

Our long-term vision is to develop VIGIL into the intelligence and coordination layer of a future space medical bay, bringing different medical technologies and specialised AI systems together in one environment.

With the right research partnerships, equipment and medical oversight, we see several possibilities.

AUTOMATED BONE-HEALTH MONITORING

One of the challenges of spending extended periods in reduced gravity is the effect it can have on bone health.

We would like future versions of VIGIL to bring together different measurements that help track changes in bone metabolism.

These could include blood and urine biomarkers, vitamin and mineral assessments, and validated imaging methods.

Compact laboratory equipment could eventually make it possible to collect and analyse some of these measurements directly during a mission.

Rather than relying on one reading, VIGIL could help organise the results over time and make changes easier for medical professionals and astronauts to understand.

These measurements would support medical assessment, not independently diagnose bone-density loss or fracture risk.

ROBOTIC ULTRASOUND FOR MUSCLE MONITORING

Muscle changes are another important concern during long-duration spaceflight.

We imagine a future system that uses compact ultrasound equipment to monitor muscle structure and size over time.

A robotic or robot-assisted ultrasound system could help position the probe consistently and collect images that can be compared throughout a mission.

Specialised software could then analyse the images, track changes and flag measurements that need further review.

This would require considerable research and testing to establish that the equipment is safe and that its measurements are reliable.

AI-COORDINATED LABORATORY SERVICES

Future space missions may need to carry more of their medical testing capabilities onboard rather than depending on laboratories on Earth.

We envision VIGIL eventually connecting with compact laboratory instruments and automated sample-processing systems.

Specialised AI agents could help coordinate approved testing procedures, check equipment quality, collect results and compare them with an astronaut's previous records.

This could make routine medical investigations more manageable during missions where communication with Earth is limited.

A TEAM OF SPECIALISED MEDICAL AI AGENTS

We believe that one general-purpose AI system should not have to handle every aspect of astronaut healthcare.

Instead, we envision specialised systems working together, each with a clearly defined role.

Doctor: Helps organise medical information, review health trends and support clinical decision-making.

Nurse: Supports regular monitoring, care routines and approved procedural guidance.

Pharmacist: Helps review medication safety, maintain medication records and support inventory management.

Psychologist: Provides structured wellbeing activities, supportive communication and guidance on accessing professional care.

Over time, additional agents could assist with laboratory equipment, ultrasound imaging, nutrition and medical supplies.

The idea is to bring these different capabilities together into one coordinated system rather than having separate tools that cannot communicate with each other.

Any high-stakes medical decision or physical intervention would still require appropriate safety controls and authorised human oversight.

5. DEVELOPMENT ROADMAP

We see VIGIL developing in stages, with each stage building on what came before.

PHASE 1: INTEGRATED MISSION HEALTH MONITORING

This is the foundation of our current prototype.

It brings together synthetic astronaut records, personal health baselines, mission timelines, physiological trends, medical reference retrieval and simulated companion interactions.

PHASE 2: ADVANCED MONITORING AND PERSONALISATION

The next step would be to explore suitable physiological sensors, structured health assessments and more reliable methods of tracking individual health changes.

We also want to investigate specialised medical models and personalised support using carefully selected data and expert-reviewed testing.

PHASE 3: MEDICAL EQUIPMENT INTEGRATION

At this stage, we would explore how VIGIL could work alongside automated laboratory instruments, bone-health monitoring systems and ultrasound-based muscle assessments.

The focus would be on making different medical technologies work together within a single platform.

PHASE 4: EARTH-INDEPENDENT MEDICAL OPERATIONS

Our long-term goal is to research a coordinated medical environment that combines specialised AI agents, robotic systems, medical equipment and clinical decision-support tools.

Each stage would need its own technical, medical, ethical and safety validation before it could be used in real missions.

6. WHAT WE HAVE ACTUALLY BUILT

We believe it is important to distinguish between what VIGIL can demonstrate today and what we hope to achieve in the future.

Our submitted public LUNA-01 demonstration is a working browser application. It uses fictional crew members and synthetic health measurements and does not require users to log in.

The current public version includes:

- An interactive 3D lunar environment.

- A mission dashboard.

- Longitudinal astronaut health records.

- A Crew Health Map.

- Four simulated Medical Companion modes.

- Educational medical references from NASA.

The public demonstration uses predefined rules to select relevant educational excerpts. It does not run a live generative AI model.

We have also developed a separate authenticated prototype that uses Gemma for bounded evidence selection. It includes server-side validation, source governance and consent-based memory controls.

Some of our larger ideas are still at the research and planning stage.

The Earth communication outage is simulated. Automated blood testing, robotic laboratory procedures, diagnostic ultrasound, specialised model fine-tuning and autonomous medical treatment are future research goals, not features we claim to have completed.

Neither version has been clinically validated or authorised to provide autonomous diagnoses or prescriptions.

7. WHY VIGIL MATTERS

As humanity prepares for longer missions and eventually more permanent operations beyond Earth, healthcare will become an increasingly important part of space exploration.

Astronauts will need more than equipment that records their vital signs. They will need systems that help them understand their health, organise medical information and access appropriate support when communication with Earth is limited.

VIGIL is our attempt to explore how these capabilities could come together.

What began as a health-monitoring concept has grown into a broader vision of connected medical technology, specialised AI and future medical robotics.

We know there is a long way to go before such a system could be used in a real space mission. But we believe it is worth starting the conversation and building the foundations today.

Because when humanity begins living beyond Earth, healthcare should not be left behind.

RESEARCH FOUNDATIONS

The scientific direction behind VIGIL is informed by the NASA Human Research Program, NASA Exploration Medical Technologies and published research into the health challenges of human spaceflight.

AI-assisted development tools supported our planning, implementation, testing and deployment. The public demonstration uses deterministic reference selection and does not claim autonomous medical capabilities.
